newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS-Indonesia rupiah down again, no intervention.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Indonesia rupiah down again, no intervention.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah was hit again on Friday as investors panicked in the aftermath of its float and pushed the unit to yet another historic low against the dollar.
By the close of trading in Jakarta, the rupiah was at 2,880/2,910 against the dollar, which was more than one percent weaker than the 2,770/90 open but off a 2,960 low.
Dealers said they waited in vain for central bank intervention to restore confidence.
The central bank, Bank Indonesia, lifted the intervention band on Thursday, effectively floating the currency, but said it reserved the right to step into the market if deemed necessary.
Edwin Png, head of treasury for Bank of America in Jakarta, said the steep falls had made the market jittery.

"I have housewives calling me up to ask about the rate," he said in the early afternoon. "Bank Indonesia should intervene now or else I see the rate going up to 3,000 later in the day and 3,200 next week."
"They should do both. They should intervene and they should tighten liquidity."

In the event, the rate did not fall that far despite the lack of intervention. But dealers and analysts said the tone of the market was weak because many Indonesian companies were scrambling to hedge their dollar exposures.
They added that volumes were thin because most investors squared positions ahead of the weekend.
Most however said the panic in the rupiah would be short-lived and that the currency would soon trade at more realistic levels, perhaps some time next week.
"We'll see the bottom end of the rupiah start to appear fairly soon," said Kevin Evans, senior analyst at ANZ Securities in Jakarta.
"I'm looking for the rupiah to come in at the end of this year somewhere between 2,700 and 2,800. We'll see it recover somewhat and then see a stable cycle after that."

"There is some nervousness onshore because a lot of corporates had not fully hedged their dollar liability and thus we may indeed go to the 3,000 level before the rupiah begins to recover towards more sustainable levels in line with its basic fundamentals," Bill Belchere, the head of Asian fixed income research at Merrill Lynch, told Reuters Financial Television.

"We do believe the fundamentals are sound, Indonesia is not like Thailand in any way," he added. "However, it's a very nervous market, you cannot contain the effect of spillover in the medium-term. However, in the longer-term we are sure Indonesia has very fine economic prospects and we would see the rupiah somewhere between 2,600 and 2,700 to the dollar."

The prolonged spell of currency weakness which has hit Southeast Asia began in May with attacks on the Thai baht. Thailand was forced to devalue its currency in July and has said it has received pledges worth $17 billion from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Asian nations.
The IMF has welcomed Indonesia's decision to allow its currency to float, saying the move would allow the country's economy to continue its recent impressive performance.

"In present circumstances, a floating exchange rate will enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies aimed at sustaining high rates of growth with financial stability," said Stanley Fischer, acting managing director of the IMF, in a statement issued in Washington.

Fischer called Indonesia's decision timely and said it came partly in response to turbulence on regional currency markets. He said floating the rupiah was "in line with Bank Indonesia's steady progress toward greater exchange rate flexibility, particularly over the last two years".
